title: Security Valuation
outcomes: Explain return concepts and estimate the required return on equity.
Value equity with dividend, earnings, free cash flow and EV methods.
Value rights, preference shares, warrants and convertibles.
Value bonds and measure duration, convexity and yield curves.
Describe money market instruments and the role of valuers.

meta.exam_tip: Match each cash flow with its rate: FCFF–WACC, FCFE/dividends–Ke, bonds–YTM.

concepts.title: Return concepts and the required return on equity
body: Valuation estimates what an asset is worth from its expected cash flows and risk. Return concepts: required return (minimum acceptable return for the risk), discount rate (rate used to compute present values) and internal rate of return (rate equating price with expected cash flows).

The equity risk premium is the extra return investors demand for holding equities over risk-free assets; estimated historically (average past excess returns) or forward-looking (e.g. implied from dividend yields and growth).

Required return on equity is often estimated with CAPM: Ke = Rf + β (Rm − Rf); alternatives include build-up methods and the dividend growth model. Discount rates must match cash flows: nominal with nominal, real with real; FCFF with WACC; FCFE and dividends with cost of equity.
concepts.analogy: The right discount rate depends on whose cash flow you are valuing.
concepts.work: With Rf 7%, β 1.2 and ERP 6%, Ke = 14.2%.

concepts.title: Valuing equity: dividends, earnings, free cash flows and EV
body: Dividend discount models: constant growth P₀ = D₁ ÷ (Ke − g); multi-stage models for high-growth then stable phases. Earnings models use P/E multiples or the earnings yield.

Free cash flow models: FCFF = EBIT(1 − t) + depreciation − capital expenditure − increase in working capital, discounted at WACC to value the firm; FCFE = FCFF − interest(1 − t) + net borrowing, discounted at Ke to value equity. FCFE suits firms that pay little dividend relative to capacity.

Enterprise value = market value of equity + debt + preference capital + minority interest − cash and equivalents. EV/Sales suits loss-making or early-stage firms; EV/EBITDA neutralises capital structure and depreciation differences.
concepts.analogy: Value the firm with FCFF and WACC, or equity with FCFE and Ke.
concepts.work: EV/EBITDA lets you compare firms with different debt levels.

concepts.title: Rights, preference shares and warrants
body: Theoretical ex-rights price (TERP) = (existing shares × cum-rights price + subscription money) ÷ total shares after issue. Value of a right per existing share = (TERP − subscription price) ÷ number of existing shares needed for one new share.
Preference shares: irredeemable value = dividend ÷ required return; redeemable value = PV of dividends + PV of redemption amount.

Warrants give the right to buy shares at a fixed price: theoretical value = (market price of share − exercise price) × shares per warrant (minimum value), with actual value usually higher due to time value. Convertible debentures are valued as straight debt plus the conversion option; conversion value = conversion ratio × share price.
concepts.analogy: Rights shift value from old shares to the new subscription — wealth is unchanged if rights are used or sold.
concepts.work: A 1-for-4 issue at ₹100 when shares trade at ₹150 gives a TERP of ₹140.

concepts.title: Bond valuation, duration and the yield curve
body: Bond value = PV of coupons + PV of redemption value at the required yield. Yield to maturity is the IRR of the bond. Prices and yields move inversely; discount bonds rise toward par as maturity nears; longer and lower-coupon bonds are more price-sensitive.

Macaulay duration is the weighted average time to receive the bond's cash flows (weights = PV of each cash flow ÷ price). Modified duration = Macaulay ÷ (1 + yield) and estimates % price change ≈ −modified duration × change in yield. Convexity corrects for curvature. Immunisation matches portfolio duration with the investment horizon so price and reinvestment effects offset.

The yield curve shows yields across maturities (normal upward, inverted, flat, humped). Term structure theories: expectations, liquidity preference and market segmentation. Zero-coupon bonds have duration equal to maturity; refunding replaces old high-coupon bonds when rates fall, if NPV is positive.
concepts.analogy: Duration is the bond's interest-rate sensitivity in years.
concepts.work: A 3-year 8% bond at 10% YTM has duration of about 2.78 years.

concepts.title: Money market instruments and the role of valuers
body: Money market instruments have maturities up to one year: call/notice money (interbank, overnight to 14 days), treasury bills (91, 182, 364 days, issued at discount), commercial bills, certificates of deposit (issued by banks), commercial paper (unsecured short-term notes of corporates), and repo/reverse repo (sale and repurchase of securities, used for liquidity management).
Yield on a discount instrument = (face value − price) ÷ price × (365 ÷ days).

Registered valuers (under the Companies Act and IBBI rules) must be independent, competent, follow valuation standards, document assumptions, avoid conflicts of interest and maintain confidentiality; their reports support transactions, insolvency proceedings and regulatory filings.
concepts.analogy: Short-term instruments manage liquidity; valuers bring independence to value.
concepts.work: A 91-day T-bill bought at ₹98 for ₹100 face yields about 8.2% a year.

illustrations.title: FCFE valuation and a rights issue
illustrations.q: (a) Prism Ltd. expects free cash flow to equity of ₹50 crore next year, growing at 6% forever. Risk-free rate 7%, beta 1.2, equity risk premium 6%. Value the equity. (b) Its shares trade at ₹150 cum-rights; it offers 1 new share for every 4 held at ₹100. Compute the theoretical ex-rights price and value of a right per existing share.
